newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Witness tells UN court Bosnian guard raped her.
newsitem.headline: Witness tells UN court Bosnian guard raped her.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb woman said on Tuesday a Moslem camp guard on trial for warcrimes at the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia raped her and incited others to do the same at the Celebici prison camp in 1992.
Weeping, and with her voice cracking with emotion, Grozdana Cecez, 47, said Hazim Delic had raped her when she arrived at the Bosnian government run camp in May 1992.
She added she had seen him beat or rape other prisoners during her three-month imprisonment at the former Yugoslav army camp in central Bosnia.

Delic, is charged along with fellow Moslems Esad Landzo and Zejnil Delalic with war crimes allegedly committed at the camp. A fourth accused, Bosnian Croat Zdravko "Pavo" Mucic, was the camp's commander.
All four deny the charges.
The trial is the first war crimes hearing since the Tokyo trials after World War Two to deal with rape and sexual assault accusations.

Delic sat expressionless as Cecez told the court of his involvement in a number of rapes other than her own -- which she had described in testimony on Monday -- assaulting fellow prisoner Milojka Antic repeatedly.
"I simply saw how, when Hazim Delic would come at noon, he would make me go into the front room. Then he raped her (Antic) in broad daylight. He would come again and take her," she said.
Cecez, whose family was scattered during the upheavals in central Bosnia during 1992, described a regime of rape, starvation and brutality at the camp.

Questioned by prosecutor Teresa McHenry, she told the court Delic had ordered her from her room at the camp and made her get into a car, even though she had complained of stomach cramps because of her period.
Fearing for her life, Cecez was driven to a hangar at the base where she was questioned by a civilian. During the questioning the man raped her.
"He said let's talk about sex, then he threw me over and started raping me.
"I took the blood with my right hand and marked his left shoulder with it to show that I really had a period. He smelled of brandy," she said falteringly.
Her experiences at the camp, where she lost 30 kilos (66 lb) in weight, took a heavy pyschological toll and drove her to the brink of suicide.

"On one occasion we were talking about committing suicide. I had a metal pin and I went into the bathroom. (Antic) took me by the shoulder and took me out of the bathroom because I was going to put the pin in the (electric) socket," Cecez said.
"I thought that if I survived I would never speak out loud again. That's the fear we Serbs felt," she said.
"Pyschologically and physically I was completely worn out. They kill you psychologically."

Cecez said on one occasion she had seen Delic beat a male Serb prisoner so hard that the baton he used had snapped and that he had continued kicking him afterwards. When the man's body was removed from his quarters the next day she was told another prisoner had strangled him.
After her release on August 31, 1992, her ordeal continued as she was forced by the authorities to identify the mutilated remains of her husband, Lazar.
Cecez could only identify him by his build and teeth as his eyes had been gouged out and his ears and nose severed.

The tribunal has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has died), 18 Croats and three Moslems. One man has been convicted and sentenced to 10 years in jail and a verdict is expected soon in another case.
